content: Sickle cell disease (SCD) is a severe monogenic disorder caused by the inheritance of two abnormal beta-globin genes. It is associated with significant complications, including severe pain, end-organ damage, pulmonary issues, and premature death. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a common and potentially severe complication in individuals with SCD. CKD is defined as structural or functional abnormalities of the kidney that persist for more than three months. Sickle cell nephropathy encompasses the range of kidney complications seen in SCD. Glomerular damage, which can lead to microalbuminuria, often begins in childhood and becomes more prevalent in adulthood. The prognosis for individuals with sickle cell nephropathy is poor due to progression to proteinuria and chronic kidney insufficiency. Approximately 12% of individuals with sickle cell nephropathy progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions aimed at preventing or reducing kidney complications or CKD in individuals with SCD. Potential interventions include red blood cell transfusions, hydroxyurea, and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs), either as monotherapy or in combination. The review included three randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a total of 385 participants. The certainty of the evidence was rated as low to very low due to concerns about bias, indirectness, and imprecision. 1. Hydroxyurea versus placebo: One RCT conducted in 2011 included 193 children aged 9 to 18 months. The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether hydroxyurea reduces or prevents the progression of kidney disease, as measured by changes in glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (mean difference [MD] 0.58 mL/min/1.73 m², 95% confidence interval [CI] −14.60 to 15.76; 142 participants; very low certainty). Hydroxyurea may improve the ability to concentrate urine (MD 42.23 mOsm/kg, 95% CI 12.14 to 72.32; 178 participants; low certainty). Hydroxyurea may have little or no effect on the incidence of SCD-related serious adverse events, including acute chest syndrome (risk ratio [RR] 0.39, 99% CI 0.13 to 1.16; 193 participants; low certainty), painful crises (RR 0.68, 99% CI 0.45 to 1.02; 193 participants; low certainty), and hospitalizations (RR 0.83, 99% CI 0.68 to 1.01; 193 participants; low certainty). No deaths were reported in either trial arm, and the study did not assess quality of life. 2. ACE inhibitors (ACEIs) versus placebo: One RCT conducted in 1998 included 22 adults with normal blood pressure and microalbuminuria. The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether captopril (an ACEI) reduces proteinuria (MD −49.00 mg/day, 95% CI −124.10 to 26.10; 22 participants; very low certainty). The trial authors reported that creatinine clearance remained constant over six months in both groups, but no comparative data were provided (very low certainty). The study did not report serious adverse events, all-cause mortality, or quality of life. 3. ACE inhibitors versus vitamin C: One RCT conducted in 2020 included 170 children aged 1 to 18 years with normal blood pressure and microalbuminuria. The study did not provide analyzable data. It is unclear whether lisinopril (an ACEI) reduces proteinuria compared to vitamin C. A significant reduction in microalbuminuria was observed in both groups after one month of treatment, but this may have been due to an overestimation of baseline microalbuminuria rather than a true treatment effect. The study did not report serious adverse events, all-cause mortality, or quality of life. No RCTs were identified that evaluated the effects of red blood cell transfusions or combination therapies on kidney complications in SCD. Additionally, no studies addressed the management of children older than 18 months or adults with any SCD genotype. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine whether hydroxyurea improves GFR or reduces hyperfiltration in young children with SCD. Hydroxyurea may improve urine concentration ability but appears to have little or no effect on acute chest syndrome, painful crises, or hospitalizations. Similarly, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether ACEIs prevent or reduce kidney complications in adults or children with normal blood pressure and microalbuminuria. The lack of adequately designed and powered studies limits the ability to draw definitive conclusions. Four ongoing trials were identified, but only one focuses on renal function as a primary outcome in the short term. Further research, particularly in older children and adults, is urgently needed to evaluate the effects of hydroxyurea, ACEIs, and red blood cell transfusions on kidney complications in SCD.
